newsitem.title: FRANCE: France says freedoms must be respected in Lebanon.
newsitem.headline: France says freedoms must be respected in Lebanon.

text.p: France called on Monday for the respect of "democratic freedoms" in Lebanon where security forces have arrested people suspected of involvement in violence which Paris says was aimed at Syrian military forces.
"The French government is convinced the Lebanese government will scrupulously abide by the rule of law," Foreign Ministry spokesman Yves Doutriaux told reporters.
"It is in no one's interest that this affair be used to restrict democratic freedoms in Lebanon," he said.

Doutriaux was replying to questions after a wave of arrests among Lebanese Christians which opposition politicians said had reached 200. The Lebanese government gave no figure for the number of arrests.

Doutriaux said Paris, which has close ties to the Beirut government but in the past supported Lebanese nationalists who accuse the present authorities of being Syrian puppets, would "not interfere in the domestic affairs of a friendly state".

Lebanese Prosecutor-general Adnan Addoum said the detentions followed increased activities by "disruptive elements" who wanted to harm Lebanon's ties with brotherly and friendly countries, an apparent reference to Syria, which props up the Beirut authorities with some 35,000 troops.
The French Foreign Ministry said the incident which had led to the crackdown was the machine-gunning of a Syrian army truck near the Christian bastion of Junieh on December 17.

Addoum had spoken of "armed attacks against civilians with hand grenades and firing with machineguns at a van carrying Syrian workers, killing the driver and wounding some passengers...distributing leaflets attacking state officials and inciting sectarian strife".

Paris-based Lebanese Christian Maronite exiles called at the weekend on French President Jacques Chirac to help "put an end to the persecution of peaceful Lebanese whose only crime is to want their country's freedom". They also want French Foreign Minister Herve de Charette to travel to Lebanon.

France, once the mandatory power in Lebanon and Syria, long saw itself as protector of the Lebanese Maronite Christians in favour of whom it first sent an expeditionary force to the area in the 1860s and later carved out modern Lebanon as a state from the Ottoman Empire.
France modified its stance in the last decade as the Christians fought among themselves and Paris sought closer ties with more powerful or richer Arab Moslem states.
